title: Scope and Limitations of the Study
content:
SCOPE AND DELIMITATION

Scope

This study focuses on the development and testing of a portable emergency safety device for motorcycle and Public Utility Vehicle (PUV) drivers in Kalibo, Aklan. The device is designed to help drivers report emergencies, detect possible crashes, and send their location to registered emergency contacts. It also includes a web-based platform where authorized users can view alerts and access recorded incidents.

The device is designed with the following features:

Two-Stage Manual SOS Activation. The device has a two-stage SOS button that allows drivers to send an emergency alert while helping prevent accidental activation.

Driver-Assistance Button. A separate button allows drivers to request assistance when they feel unsafe or need help while on the road.

Automatic Crash Detection. The device uses an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to detect possible crashes by checking sudden changes in acceleration, changes in vehicle orientation, and whether the vehicle stops moving after a possible impact. A 10-second cancellation period allows the driver to cancel the alert if no emergency has occurred.

GPS Location Reporting. The device uses a GPS receiver to determine the vehicle's location and include it in emergency alerts.

SMS Emergency Alerts. The device sends text messages to registered contacts. Each message contains the event type, device ID, date and time, GPS coordinates, and a map link. A secondary contact is also included as a backup.

Audible Alarm. The device includes an audible alarm to help alert people nearby when an emergency occurs.

Backup Battery and Power Monitoring. A backup battery allows the device to continue operating when the main power source becomes unavailable. The device also monitors its battery level and provides warnings when the battery is low.

Status Indicators and Event Recording. The device has status indicators that show its operating condition. It also saves important events with timestamps so the recorded information can be reviewed later.

Web-Based IoT Monitoring Platform. The platform allows authorized users to manage registered devices, view emergency alerts and reported locations, and access stored incident records.

The study will test the device under controlled conditions to check how well its features work. The tests will cover crash detection, false alarms, GPS accuracy, SMS delivery, response time, data transmission, event recording, audible alarm performance, backup power operation, and the usability of the web-based platform.

Delimitation

This study is limited to the development and testing of the proposed device and its web-based platform in Kalibo, Aklan. Testing will involve simulated crash-like situations and normal driving conditions. Actual road crashes and dangerous driving situations will not be part of the testing.

The accuracy of GPS location reporting may vary depending on satellite signals and the surrounding environment. The delivery of text messages and the transfer of data to the web platform also depend on the availability and quality of the cellular network. The operating time of the backup battery will depend on its capacity and the device's power consumption.

The driver-assistance feature requires the driver to press the button when assistance is needed. It does not detect or diagnose medical conditions, psychological concerns, or other personal conditions that may affect the driver.

The study will not include smoke or fire detection, engine or engine-compartment temperature monitoring, vehicle battery condition monitoring, theft or unauthorized movement detection, geofencing, passenger-side emergency buttons, physical tamper detection, voice communication, physiological stress monitoring, or machine-learning-based crash classification.

The device is intended to help drivers report emergencies and provide important incident information. It cannot prevent road crashes, guarantee the arrival of emergency responders, or replace existing emergency services. The web-based platform is limited to the monitoring, notification, and record-management features developed for this study. Advanced fleet management and predictive analytics are not included.

title: Overview of the Current State of Technology
content:
Overview of the current state of the technology
For over half a century, emergency response operations managed by Local and Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Offices (LDRRMOs/MDRRMOs) have faced a persistent challenge: excessive emergency notification latency.
Historically, emergency response relies entirely on manual reporting. Following a vehicular collision, emergency medical services (EMS) and traffic enforcement units are dispatched only after receiving telephone calls or walk-in reports from victims, eyewitnesses, or passing motorists.
Manual Emergency Reporting
Problem Addressed the fundamental need to inform authorities that an incident occurred so rescue units can be deployed.
Outcome and Limitations: Manual reporting requires no capital expenditure for specialized vehicular or roadside infrastructure. However, it introduces substantial notification delays that frequently exceed the critical "Golden Hour" of medical care. Manual reports are inherently subjective, prone to panic-induced errors, and often lack precise geographical coordinates particularly when collisions occur along unmonitored highway segments, rural corridors, or late-night hours.
First-Generation Embedded Hardware Solutions
To eliminate human reporting delays, early automated crash detection initiatives introduced low-cost, standalone embedded hardware prototypes. These systems pair microcontrollers (e.g., Arduino or Raspberry Pi platforms) with accelerometers, vibration sensors, GPS modules, and GSM shields.
Specific Improvement Introduced: Automated detection eliminated reliance on human eyewitnesses by continuously monitoring acceleration thresholds and automatically dispatching an SMS containing raw GPS coordinates upon impact.
Outcome and Limitations: While proving the feasibility of automated impact sensing, standalone hardware units suffer from high rates of false positives (triggered by sudden braking, speed bumps, or dropping the device) and operate in functional isolation. Sending plain-text SMS messages to private contacts or arbitrary phone numbers fails to establish an authenticated, direct link with municipal emergency dispatchers, leading to unverified or lost emergency alerts.

Contemporary Technological Paradigms & Solutions
Modern developments in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) have split into two primary domains: commercial fleet telematics and offline spatial predictive modeling.
Commercial Telematics and Fleet Management Platforms
In response to regulatory mandates—such as the Department of Transportation (DOTr) Public Utility Vehicle Modernization Program (PUVMP) and Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) guidelines in the Philippines—modern Public Utility Vehicles (PUVs) are increasingly equipped with GPS tracking and onboard telematics. Advanced international implementations further incorporate multi-sensor verification (e.g., driver for physiological monitoring, acoustic sensing, and pressure sensors) or cloud-based Deep Learning models to process complex vehicular telemetry. 
Specific Improvement Introduced: Replaced basic SMS alerts with continuous real-time fleet monitoring, route tracking, driver behavior analysis, and multi-sensor impact validation.
Outcome and Limitations: Existing fleet management platforms are engineered primarily for commercial fleet operators, route compliance, fuel monitoring, and driver management not for municipal emergency response dispatch. When an impact event occurs, commercial telematics software retains the data within proprietary, closed-loop cloud systems that do not interface directly with local government emergency response dashboards. Furthermore, foreign platforms dependent on continuous high-speed cloud connectivity and costly multi-sensor arrays present prohibitive capital and operational expenses for local public transit operators.
Spatial Analytics and Predictive Blackspot Mapping
Concurrently, transport safety research heavily emphasizes the use of Machine Learning (ML) classification algorithms alongside spatial clustering techniques, such as Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). These approaches process historical crash logs, roadway geometry, traffic volumes, and temporal factors to map and forecast accident-prone locations ("blackspots"). 
Specific Improvement Introduced: Shifted road safety management from purely reactive responses to data-driven proactive planning, identifying high-risk zones and optimizing enforcement schedules. 
Outcome & Limitations: Although predictive spatial modeling provides essential empirical data for long-term urban planning and infrastructure design, these methods are inherently reactive and offline. Historical analytics cannot monitor active transit fleets in real time, detect an ongoing collision, or automatically trigger the dispatch of local emergency response assets during an active incident.
Rationale and Problem Statement
Despite decades of iterative technological developments, a distinct operational gap persists in municipal road safety management: 
Current crash detection solutions remain fragmented. Standalone hardware devices transmit unverified SMS alerts to private phone numbers, while advanced telematics store telemetry within closed commercial software inaccessible to local first responders. Consequently, municipal emergency units (such as MDRRMOs) remain dependent on delayed manual notifications to discover and verify road crashes.
Public Utility Vehicles (PUVs) carry high commuter volumes daily, rendering crashes involving these vehicles at high-risk events with potential for mass casualties. The absence of an integrated, automated reporting channel connecting PUVs to the local Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) directly results in, Prolonged Emergency Response Latency, first responders waste critical minutes awaiting manual incident reports from passersby or victims.
 With geographical Ambiguity, dispatchers have trouble pinpointing precise crash coordinates along unmonitored or rural transit routes. 
Lack of Incident Verification, the absence of real-time impact telematics prevents command centers from assessing incident severity prior to asset deployment. 
Proposed Solution and Research Contribution
The proposed study, PUV Emergency Detection, Alert, and Monitoring System with MDRRMO Integration, directly addresses this technological and operational void.
Rather than replicating isolated hardware prototypes or proprietary commercial telematics, this research establishes an end to end framework that integrates onboard vehicular impact detection with a dedicated, real-time MDRRMO emergency web dashboard. By streaming authenticated collision alerts, impact severity metrics, and live GPS coordinates directly to municipal dispatchers, the proposed system eliminates reliance on manual reporting chains, mitigates false-alarm delays, and enables rapid, data-driven emergency deployment for public utility vehicle safety.

title: Review of Related Literature/Studies/Systems
content:
REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES
This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of previous research, foundational theories, and technological frameworks that establish the context for the PUV Emergency Detection, Alert, and Monitoring System with MDRRMO Integration. The literature reviewed examines public utility vehicle safety, IoT-enabled emergency detection mechanisms, wireless communication technologies, and municipal disaster risk reduction management integration.
A. Related Literature
Public Utility Vehicle (PUV) Safety and Security
Public Utility Vehicles (PUVs) serve as the backbone of mass transportation, carrying millions of commuters daily. However, passenger safety remains a critical concern due to potential road accidents, mechanical failures, medical emergencies onboard, or security threats such as robberies and assaults (Department of Transportation [DOTr], 2023). According to safety transport literature, traditional public transit lacks real-time communication channels between drivers, passengers, and emergency response units during in-transit crises. In many cases, emergency notifications rely on delayed cellular phone calls or manual bystander reporting, which significantly increases response latency and compromises passenger survival rates during critical incidents (Santos et al., 2022).
Emergency Detection Mechanisms and IoT Integration
The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) into vehicular safety has transformed transit monitoring. Modern embedded systems utilize multi-sensor configurations—such as inertial measurement units (accelerometers and gyroscopes) for collision detection, panic buttons for manual driver/passenger alerts, and temperature or smoke sensors for onboard hazard monitoring (Kiran et al., 2020). When an emergency trigger is activated, automated sensor nodes instantly capture telemetry data and pair it with live geographic coordinates via Global Positioning System (GPS) modules, enabling precise tracking of the distressed vehicle (Omar et al., 2024). 
Microcontrollers and Wireless Data Transmission
Microcontrollers act as the core processing units for vehicular emergency nodes. Platforms such as the Arduino Uno or ESP32 provide reliable digital and analog processing capabilities, interfacing seamlessly with GSM/GPRS modules, LoRa, or Wi-Fi shields to transmit distress packets over cellular networks (Monk, 2017). Literature emphasizes that utilizing cellular communication gateways allows mobile vehicle units to transmit emergency packets across wide municipal distances directly to centralized servers without requiring proprietary repeater infrastructure. 
Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) Integration
In the Philippine setting, the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) serves as the primary frontline agency responsible for disaster management, search and rescue, and emergency medical dispatch at the local government level (National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council [NDRRMC], 2023). Integrating PUV emergency systems directly into an MDRRMO command center bridges the gap between on-road incidents and official municipal response units. Literature highlights that centralized dashboards equipped with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) allow dispatchers to visualize incoming distress signals in real time, optimize ambulance or police routing, and coordinate rapid tactical deployments (Garcia, 2024). 
Related Studies
Foreign Studies
International studies broaden these hardware concepts by incorporating secondary verification steps, smartphone sensors, and cloud-based artificial intelligence. Sarker et al. [58] established a smart crash recognition, area tracking, and notification platform that instantly detects a crash whenever it happens. The GPS module discovers the precise area of the crash, and the GSM component transmits a notice, such as a link to the area on Google Maps, to the closest police station and medical center, enabling them to verify the location. They can also discover the quickest route to the crash location and attempt to accelerate the rescue procedure.  
Chaithanya et al. [85] introduced a platform that, once a crash is detected, triggers a buzzer. If the driver does not respond to the buzzer within a fixed time period, the GPS sensor updates the location via Wi-Fi, along with eye blink readings, heartbeat data, and information about which side the victim has fallen. Immediately after the accident, a GSM sensor transmits the location and cloud link address to the mobile phone connected to the platform. Instantly after an SMS, a notification call can be received through predetermined emergency contacts, and the closest hospital can be informed about the victim’s location.   
Alkinani et al. [86] suggested a crash recognition platform for an intelligent city, which is suitable for any automobile and more affordable. They established an android program which gathers information associated with audio, pressure, gravitational force, velocity, and area of the crash through the mobile phone. The magnitude of velocity helps enhance the precision of crash recognition. A navigation platform was developed to notify the family, the closest medical center, and the police station. 
Kumar et al. [87] suggested a simulation model that finds crashes utilizing several modules. The circuit, incorporating the module, is integrated with an Arduino microcontroller created and simulated using the Proteus Simulation Program. Whenever the crash is actually recognized, an SMS can be delivered to relatives via the application. Virtual serial port emulator software links to the Proteus Simulation Program as well as the IoT system. The Blynk IoT System is actually utilized to design the prototype of the Android program that identifies crashes. Sumathy et al. [88] created an automobile crash notifying and discovery platform, which can save people from hazardous highway crashes, particularly in remote locations where individual activities are limited. The GPS module provides precise location details and sends them via SMS to the closest police station, EMS, medical center, and the victim’s relatives. The EMS can be reached instantly at the crash location by utilizing the area information, and fast medical assistance can be given to the victim.  
Pathik et al. [14] suggested a smart crash recognition and recovery platform that mimics the cognitive features of the individual brain, utilizing AI and IoT systems. An IoT system can be designed to locate the crash as well as gather all details, for example, location, gravitational force, pressure, and velocity, and transmit this information to the cloud. As soon as the crash is recognized through the DL method, all the nearest emergency services, for example, the medical center, mechanics, and police station, can be contacted. 
Local Studies 
In the Philippines, local researchers frequently focus on low-cost embedded hardware prototypes to overcome infrastructure gaps. Balcita et al. (2019) engineered a real-time vehicle accident alert platform using an Arduino microcontroller interfaced with a multi-axis accelerometer, a vibration sensor, a NEO-6M GPS module, and a SIM900A GSM shield. Upon sensing an acceleration threshold spike or structural shock indicative of a crash, the system extracts precise GPS coordinates and automatically dispatches an emergency SMS containing a Google Maps link to pre-designated responders, drastically reducing emergency notification delays in unmonitored road segments. 
In a broader regional evaluation, Velasco et al. (2021) examined traffic incident criticality across the CALABARZON transport network using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and multi-factor statistical modeling. Their findings demonstrated that vehicle size variations, speed differentials across lanes, and driver age significantly influence crash severity levels, establishing an empirical foundation for localized speed management and highway enforcement policies.  
Ballarta (2023) conducted a spatial cluster analysis focusing on public utility vehicles (PUVs) along Commonwealth Avenue in Quezon City using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) under the UP National Center for Transportation Studies (UP NCTS). The study mapped high-density incident clusters to determine critical spatial and temporal patterns, identifying peak commuting hours and major merging corridors as the primary hot spots for vehicular damage and injury crashes.  
Duran et al. (2024) established a data-driven framework utilizing machine learning algorithms—specifically Decision Tree, Naïve Bayes, and Rule Induction—to identify and forecast accident-prone locations (blackspots) in Silang, Cavite. By evaluating historical crash logs, their Decision Tree model achieved an accuracy of 89.84% in predicting incident occurrences based on parameters such as trip duration, day of the week, and highway geometry, providing local transport authorities with actionable insights for proactive road safety interventions.  
Similarly, a local study (2024) developed an IoT-based smart helmet system designed to protect motorcycle delivery riders from delayed emergency assistance. The system integrates an embedded accelerometer, an ATTM336H GPS module, and Firebase cloud integration to continuously monitor movement and impact. By leveraging decision threshold algorithms, the smart helmet achieved a 90% accuracy rate in distinguishing actual collision impacts from non-crash motions, instantly transmitting live location coordinates to emergency contacts and logistics services. 
Research Gaps
The PUV Emergency Detection, Alert, and Monitoring System with MDRRMO Integration aims to provide a localized, end-to-end safety solution for public transit. While existing foreign studies, such as those by Sravani et al. (2025) and Omar et al. (2024), focus broadly on general vehicle accident tracking or private vehicle telematics, they rarely address the specific operational dynamics of Philippine Public Utility Vehicles (such as jeepneys and local commuter vans) nor do they integrate directly with municipal disaster management infrastructure.
In Addition, prior local implementations (Garcia, 2024; Reyes, 2023) often concentrate on SMS-based notifications sent to generic mobile numbers rather than a centralized, real-time monitoring dashboard housed within a formal municipal agency. The proposed system fills these critical gaps by combining low-cost onboard sensor and panic modules with direct cellular transmission to an MDRRMO-integrated command center dashboard, ensuring that public utility vehicle emergencies receive immediate, coordinated municipal response. 

Conceptual Framework


As illustrated in the conceptual framework, this study identifies the PUV Emergency Detection, Alert, and Monitoring System with MDRRMO Integration as the independent variable (IV), encompassing the system's design and operational parameters, which include onboard sensor and panic button configurations, microcontroller processing efficiency, and cellular data transmission protocols. The dependent variable (DV) is represented by system performance, measured through emergency detection accuracy, alert transmission latency, and MDRRMO command dashboard response speed.
The purpose of this study is to evaluate how effectively the integration of automated PUV emergency hardware and municipal command monitoring improves emergency response efficiency. It is hypothesized that optimized sensor triggers and direct integration with the MDRRMO will minimize emergency notification latency, enhance dispatcher situational awareness, and provide a reliable, scalable safety framework for public transportation.
